name: Opisthorchis viverrini

taxonomy.rank_note: Reference groups can include multiple species. Protozoan higher-rank systems differ; the lineage is provided without forcing every clade into a class rank.

morphology: Egg: approximately 19–30 × 10–20 µm; yellow-brown, embryonated, with an operculum, shoulders and a small opposite-end knob.
Adults occupy bile ducts; metacercariae in fish are infective to humans.

transmission.detail: Eggs reach water in feces; development in snails precedes cercarial infection of freshwater fish. Eating fish containing viable metacercariae introduces flukes that mature in bile ducts.

life_cycle.detail: Eggs leave the definitive host in feces.
A freshwater snail ingests eggs; larval stages develop.
Cercariae leave the snail and encyst as metacercariae in fish.
Eating infected undercooked fish introduces larvae that mature in bile ducts.

hosts: Definitive: humans and fish-eating mammals, including cats and dogs. Intermediate: freshwater snail, then cyprinid fish.
distribution: Focal transmission in Thailand and the Mekong region, associated with raw or undercooked freshwater fish.
clinical_significance: Light infection may be silent; chronic infection can cause biliary inflammation and obstruction and is associated with cholangiocarcinoma.
specimen: Embryonated eggs in stool; adult worms are uncommon routine specimens.
diagnostics: Stool wet mount and concentration; inspect opercular detail around 400× total magnification.
Molecular testing can help resolve small-fluke infections when available.
differential_diagnosis: Eggs overlap Clonorchis and minute intestinal flukes; morphology alone may not establish species.
Dataset OV sub-variants should remain appearance attributes unless independently verified as biological taxa.
review_status: Source-compiled educational content; not independently clinically validated
description: Opisthorchis viverrini — Southeast Asian liver fluke. Light infection may be silent; chronic infection can cause biliary inflammation and obstruction and is associated with cholangiocarcinoma.

annotation_guidance: Record specimen, stage, stain, objective/total magnification, pixel calibration, source image and reviewer certainty.
Native crops of 200–650 pixels do not determine biological size. Retain µm-per-pixel calibration before resizing.
Split training, validation and test data by patient/specimen; keep related crops in the same split.
Keep damaged or ambiguous objects uncertain. Molecular confirmation of a mixed specimen does not assign every pictured object a species.
